title: Strong as death

cards: A seal is a small thing: a carved stone or a ring, pressed into wax or clay, and the mark it leaves says, this is mine, this comes from me. Near the end of the Song of Songs, one lover asks to become one.
Not to be given one, or to wear one: to be the seal, pressed onto the other's heart and arm. And in the same breath, the poem gives love a much bigger rival than sweetness or patience.

teach.b: Here is the verse in the King James: "Set me as a seal upon thine heart, as a seal upon thine arm: for love is strong as death; jealousy is cruel as the grave." First, the seal.

The speaker doesn't ask to be remembered fondly. She asks to be the mark itself, on the heart where feeling lives and on the arm where work gets done: love meant to show, inside and out. Second, the comparison.
Death is a force nobody bargains with, and it doesn't let go. Love, the poem says, is just as strong.

teach.h: STRONG AS DEATH, CRUEL AS THE GRAVE.
teach.b: And it isn't only gentle: jealousy is cruel as the grave, and its coals are "coals of fire." Third, the water.
The next verse adds: "Many waters cannot quench love, neither can the floods drown it." Love is the fire the floods can't put out. Fourth, how it's read.

teach.h: LOVERS, GOD AND ISRAEL, OR THE SOUL.
teach.b: Read plainly, the Song is love poetry between two lovers, and some readers take it that way.
Jewish tradition has also read it as the love between God and Israel; the Mishnah records Rabbi Akiva calling the Song the holy of holies among the scriptures.
Christian readers have heard Christ and the church, or God and the soul. These readings sit side by side. Whichever you hear, the claim is bold: love isn't the soft thing in the room.

how: Some Jewish communities read the Song of Songs in the synagogue during Passover, and lines from its eighth chapter are read at some weddings, Jewish and Christian.

games.q: you're writing a love poem and need one thing to compare love's strength to. the poem in the Song picks...
games.why: death: love is strong as death. it picks a force nobody bargains with, one that doesn't let go.

practice: Choose one person you love and rarely tell, a partner, a parent, a child, a friend, and let their face come.
Find the one plain sentence you've been too shy, too busy or too cool to say: I love you, I'm proud of you, you changed my life.
Say it silently a few times, slowly, until it feels less strange, and if you pray, let it become a prayer for them.

wordCard.voice: Seal. The Song of Songs' image for love: pressed onto the heart and the arm, a mark meant to show both inside and out. Today's word.

orig.note: Hebrew: strong as death is love.

carryVoice: Your line: many waters cannot quench love. A fire the floods can't put out. That's day eight hundred twenty-nine.
